opus-5.5.text:
I think what struck me first was just the sense that there was a whole world living inside the screen. As a kid I played games on our family computer, and I remember being amazed that you could walk around, the lighting would change, water would ripple, and somehow all of it was being created by the machine in real time. It didn't feel like watching a movie; it felt alive, because it responded to you.

And pretty quickly that amazement turned into curiosity: how does this actually work? How does a computer know what a shadow should look like, or how smoke should move? I didn't have the vocabulary back then, but I was basically asking the question that graphics and physical simulation try to answer: how do you describe the real world precisely enough that a computer can recreate it?

I think that's what hooked me. Graphics sits at this really beautiful intersection. There's math and physics underneath, there's a lot of engineering to make it fast, and then at the end you get something visual and emotional that anyone can appreciate. You don't need to understand the equations to look at a beautiful frame and feel something. That combination of rigor and visible, immediate reward was incredibly attractive to me, and honestly it still is today. It's a big part of why I ended up working on simulation and eventually on building tools like Taichi: I wanted to make it easier for more people to create those worlds themselves.

r001.rationale: The response describes being fascinated by a responsive world created inside a computer and mentions math and physics, but it does not identify arithmetic operations as the means of creating that world.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. When I was a kid playing games, what really got me wasn't the gameplay itself so much as the question of how any of it was possible. You'd see water rippling, or smoke drifting, or a character's shadow moving across a wall, and I kept thinking: there's no water inside this machine. There's no light. It's just a chip doing arithmetic, and somehow out of all those numbers comes something that looks and behaves like the real world.

That gap fascinated me. On one side you have physics, which is messy and continuous and infinite. On the other you have a computer, which is discrete and finite and quite dumb in a sense. Graphics is the art of bridging those two, of figuring out what you can throw away and what you absolutely must keep so that a person's eye still believes it. I found that a beautiful problem.

And then there was the hands-on part. When I started programming, the first time I drew a triangle on screen and then made it rotate, that feedback loop was addictive. In a lot of computing you write code and the result is a number in a log file. In graphics you write code and the result is something you can see, and often something you can see is wrong, and the wrongness is itself interesting. Why does the fluid explode? Why does the cloth pass through the table? Debugging those failures taught me more about numerical methods than any textbook.

So I'd say it was two things coming together: a kid's wonder at seeing physical phenomena recreated from nothing, and the realization that I could actually participate in building that illusion. That combination pretty much set the direction for everything I've done since, including the work on simulation and on making it easier for other people to write this kind of code without needing to be an expert in GPUs.

r001.rationale: The response says that as a child Hu wondered how a computer chip doing arithmetic could produce visuals that looked and behaved like the real world.

astra-6.text: What fascinated me was that a computer could create an entire world you could interact with. As a child playing video games, I kept wondering how the images appeared on the screen—how you could move through a scene and everything would change with you. I wanted to understand what was happening behind those images. That curiosity was what drew me toward computer graphics.

r001.rationale: The response says a computer could create an interactive world, but it does not identify arithmetic operations inside the computer as the means of creating it.

sol-6.1.text: What fascinated me was that a computer could create an entire world on a screen, and you could interact with it. You press a button, something moves, and the world responds. As a kid, I didn’t understand how any of that worked, but I really wanted to know how those images were made and whether I could create something like that myself.

r001.rationale: The response says a computer could create an interactive world on screen, but does not identify arithmetic operations inside the computer as the source of that fascination.
